text: Alaska is home to many Native peoples, each with its own language and way of eating. The Alaska Native Heritage Center groups them into five regions: Iñupiaq and St. Lawrence Island Yupik in the north, Yup'ik and Cup'ik in the southwest, Unangax̂ and Alutiiq in the Aleutians and Southcentral, Athabascans in the Interior, and Eyak, Tlingit, Haida and Tsimshian in the Southeast.

Food comes from the land and water close to home: [[Salmon]] and other fish, [[Seal oil]] and sea mammals on the coast, [[Caribou]] and [[Moose]] inland, and berries and greens picked in summer. Hunting, fishing, gathering and sharing with family and Elders are still at the center of how people eat today.

text: The Alutiiq, or Sugpiaq, live from Prince William Sound to Kodiak Island and the Alaska Peninsula. Like their Unangax̂ neighbors, their food is tied to the water: [[Salmon]] smoked and dried, halibut, seal, shellfish and seaweed, with berries and greens from the land.

text: Anishinaabe oral tradition tells of a journey west to the place where food grows on water. That food is [[Wild rice|manoomin]], wild rice, and it still feeds Ojibwe communities in Minnesota, Wisconsin and Michigan in body and spirit. At harvest, ricers pole or paddle small boats through the beds and knock the ripe grain in with cedar sticks, going back again and again as it ripens.

Late winter is sugarbush time, when families return to the same maple stands, some kept for generations, to boil sap into [[Maple syrup|syrup]] and sugar. Maple sugar seasons food, and sugar cakes molded into people, animals and moons are given as gifts.

text: Athabascan peoples live across Interior Alaska, and their lives follow the big rivers like the Yukon and Tanana, which serve as roads and as a source of food. [[Salmon]] and [[Whitefish]] are caught and dried in summer, [[Moose]] and [[Caribou]] are hunted in fall, and berries are picked and put away.
The University of Alaska Museum's guide calls sharing the most important part of Athabascan subsistence living. People who have moved away still return home to harvest.

text: Aymara families farm the Bolivian highlands, 3,000 to 4,000 meters up, where the sun is strong and the nights freeze. After the [[Potato|potato]] harvest, they sort the crop three ways: to eat soon, to plant next year, and to turn into [[Chuño]]. On frosty nights in June and July those potatoes are left out to freeze, then trodden to squeeze out the water, peeled and dried hard in the sun, and they can keep for decades. Tunta starts the same way but is soaked in a running river, which turns it white.

On Lake Titicaca, Aymara fishers have eaten karachi, a tiny native fish, for thousands of years, fried with salt or added to soups, and trade it for [[Quinoa]] and potatoes on market days. Overfishing and trout, brought into the lake in the 1930s, now threaten it.

text: [[Acorn|Acorns]] are a staple for many California nations. They are cracked, pounded into flour with a stone mortar and pestle, and washed with water to leach out the bitter tannins. The flour is cooked into [[Acorn mush]] in a watertight basket with hot stones, stirred with a wooden paddle so it doesn't burn. Hupa, Pomo, Karuk and Yurok weavers still make acorn baskets, and carvers still make mush paddles.

Cooks today bring the same foods to new tables. In Berkeley, Vincent Medina (Muwekma Ohlone) and Louis Trevino (Rumsen Ohlone) run Café Ohlone, serving acorn soup and acorn flour brownies alongside venison, chia, mushrooms and native berries.

text: Cherokee people live in northeastern Oklahoma, home of the Cherokee Nation, and in western North Carolina, home of the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians. [[Kanuchi]], a soup made from pounded hickory nuts, is still served at traditional tables and stomp grounds in Oklahoma, and the nuts are gathered in fall before the first frost.

Spring wild onion dinners bring wild onions and eggs together with [[Hominy|hominy]], beans, grape dumplings, kanuchi, fry bread and corn bread. In North Carolina, cooks simmer a [[Three Sisters]] stew of corn, beans and squash, and make an old style chestnut bread: corn cooked with wood ash, ground, mixed with chestnuts, wrapped in leaves and boiled.

text: [[Salmon]], berries, elk and roots are the core of the Coast Salish diet around the Salish Sea. Muckleshoot guidelines call for a traditional meal like roasted salmon once a week, and intertribal [[Camas]] harvests bring Elders and youth together.

The Muckleshoot Food Sovereignty Project brings huckleberries, nettles, camas, salmon and elk back into everyday meals through classes, gardens and seminars, and cooks try new forms too, like elk burgers and huckleberry smoothies. At Nisqually, a community garden gives citizens free produce and syrups made from nettle, elderberry and fir tips.

text: Diné people live across the Navajo Nation in the Four Corners, and corn is at the heart of the table. [[Blue corn]] is cooked into mush, dumplings and bread, often with juniper ash stirred in, and fresh corn is ground, wrapped in husks and baked in a pit as [[Kneel down bread]]. Gardens grow corn, beans, squash and melons, and families travel to gather wild sumac berries, chokecherries and banana yucca.

Sheep have been part of Diné life since the 1600s, so much that a well known Diné saying calls sheep life itself. [[Lamb and mutton|Mutton]] stew with potatoes, carrots and sometimes [[Hominy]] is a classic, served with [[Frybread]] or tortillas. Flour, sugar and coffee came after 1868 and are still in Diné kitchens, while summits and cooking classes pass the older recipes to younger cooks.

text: For the Eeyou of Eeyou Istchee, in the James Bay region of Quebec, the year follows the hunt. In spring, goose break empties the towns as families head to their bush camps, children learn to call geese, and goose is roasted slowly over an open fire for hours, twisting on a cord as it cooks.

[[Moose]], [[Caribou]], bear, beaver, snowshoe hare, ducks, ptarmigan and fish are all traditional foods, along with blueberries, cranberries, raspberries and strawberries. The Cree Nation Government and Cree Board of Health track how a changing climate affects each of them.

text: The Garinagu were exiled from St. Vincent and settled along the Caribbean coast of Central America, and the largest Garifuna community outside Central America is in New York City, mostly in the South Bronx. Their kitchen runs on [[Cassava]], green and ripe [[Plantain (cooking)|plantains]], green bananas, [[Coconut milk]] and fish.

[[Casabe|Ereba]], cassava bread, is women's work that takes days: the roots are peeled, grated and strained, and the flour is spread in thin rounds on a hot griddle, then shared with family and neighbors. Its color is the yellow stripe on the Garifuna flag. [[Hudut]] is plantain pounded smooth and served with falmo, fish soup made with coconut milk. Darasa are [[Tamale|tamales]] made with green banana instead of corn, and durudia are thick tortillas made with coconut milk.

text: For the Guaraní, [[Maize|corn]], avaxi, is sacred. Mbyá families in Brazil's Atlantic Forest keep old varieties like avaxi etei, and some foods are meant for certain times: one corn is recommended for new mothers, eaten with purple [[Sweet potato|sweet potato]]. Jera Guarani and community elders gathered corn recipes in a book called Ara Pyau, new time.

Mbyá women pound corn into dough with a pestle for a corn cake baked in a clay pot over coals in a hole in the ground, covered with banana leaves, and they make [[Chipá|chipa]] too. Long before wheat arrived, the Guaraní relied on [[Cassava|manioc]] as much as on corn, and in Paraguay chipa of manioc flour is still baked in a tatakua, a brick and mud oven whose Guaraní name means fire hole.

text: On the islands of Guna Yala, off Panama's Caribbean coast, meals center on the sea. Tule masi is a soup of fish and [[Plantain (cooking)|plantain]], fish caught the same day comes with coconut rice, and coconut water is drunk from a nut cut from the palm just before.

Fish is still a daily food for many island families, and many have [[Cacao|cacao]] every day, though researchers working on Ustupu and Ogobsucum found fried and packaged foods spreading fast. At big festivals, women stir huge pots of [[Chicha]] made from sugarcane juice, herbs and corn.

text: The Kaigani Haida live on southern Prince of Wales Island, around Hydaburg, with most Haida across the border in Haida Gwaii. Like their Tlingit neighbors, they eat from the forest and the sea: [[Salmon]], halibut, shellfish, seaweed, [[Herring]] eggs and berries.

text: For the Haudenosaunee, among them the Seneca, Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga and Tuscarora, white corn has been prized for about a thousand years. It grows with beans and squash as the [[Three Sisters]], and women have long led nearly every step of growing and preparing it.

The corn is planted, picked and husked by hand, braided and hung to dry, then hulled, traditionally with hardwood ash, into [[Hominy|hulled corn]] for soups and stews. Roasted and stone ground, it becomes a nutty flour for mush, bread and baking. At Ganondagan in Victor, New York, the Iroquois White Corn Project grows it and encourages Haudenosaunee families to eat it every day, not only on special occasions.

text: On the mesas of northeastern Arizona, Hopi farmers grow corn, and [[Blue corn]] is the base of [[Piki]], a paper-thin bread of cornmeal, ash and water spread by hand on a hot stone. Hopi women make it, a skill that takes years to learn, and a well kept piki stone passes from mother to daughter.
Piki is everyday food, easy to carry to the fields, and visitors are often offered a fresh roll. It also marks weddings, baby namings and other ceremonies.

text: The Iñupiat live across Alaska's far north and northwest, from the Arctic coast to the Kobuk and Noatak rivers. Life there still turns around the [[Whale]], walrus, [[Seal oil|seal]], [[Caribou]] and fish.

Whaling communities share [[Muktuk]], whale skin with its layer of fat, through the year, and frozen or dried fish dipped in [[Seal oil]] is an everyday food. [[Akutaq]], whipped fat mixed with berries, is made for gatherings.

sources.name: Alaska Native Heritage Center
University of Alaska Museum of the North, Alaska Native cultures guide

Iñupiaq foodways.area: North Slope and Northwest Arctic, Alaska

text: Kalo, or [[Taro]], is honored as an elder brother. It grows in loʻi, terraces flooded with water led from streams, and pounded and fermented into [[Poi]], it's part of almost every traditional Hawaiian meal. People show it respect: no harsh words while planting or eating it, and the poi bowl is covered if business comes up at the table.

Food traditionally came from the ahupuaʻa, land divisions running from the mountains to the sea. Upland forests gave ʻulu, [[Breadfruit]], and gardens gave ʻuala ([[Sweet potato]]), sugarcane and maiʻa (banana), while stone-walled loko iʻa, fishponds, raised fish along the shore, fed partly with kalo peels. Community groups are restoring loʻi kalo and fishponds on Maui, Molokaʻi and Oʻahu, and growers are planting far more ʻulu.

text: Kichwa families in Ecuador's Amazon grow food in the chakra, a forest garden that FAO lists as a Globally Important Agricultural Heritage System. In Alto Tena, a chakra holds lumu, [[Cassava|yuca]], kakau, [[Cacao|cacao]], and its wild cousins, chunta palm fruit, kumal, [[Sweet potato|sweet potato]], uchu muyu chiles, manduru, [[Achiote|achiote]], and dozens of forest fruits and nuts.

Visitors are welcomed with [[Chicha]] of yuca, which women mostly make. The boiled roots are mashed in a wooden trough, chewed and returned so saliva breaks down the starch, then left to ferment for a couple of days or longer, thinned with water and served in a clay bowl called a mucawa. [[Guayusa]], a native leaf, is traditionally brewed and sipped in the morning, and Kichwa entrepreneur Esthela Noteno now bottles it from her grandmother's recipe.

text: Lakota life on the Northern Plains centers on [[Bison]], tatanka, a sacred animal that gives food, clothing, shelter and tools. Meat is dried in thin strips, and dried meat mixed with fat and chokecherries becomes wasna, the Lakota form of [[Pemmican]], made to last through hard winters. Corn came by trade with the Mandan villages.

Wild berries, traditionally chokecherries, are cooked into [[Wojapi]], eaten with [[Frybread]] or alongside meat. Today bison are returning to tribal lands, and Oglala Lakota chef Sean Sherman cooks with Indigenous foods only, leaving out wheat flour, dairy and cane sugar.

text: Mapuche cooking follows the seasons, built on grains and legumes gathered through the year. In the Araucanía, piñones, the big seeds of the araucaria tree, are cooked, sautéed with garlic, oregano and salt, and finished with [[Merkén]], smoked chile ground with spices. Spring brings digüeñes, chewy mushrooms that grow on oak trees, for salads, stews and empanadas, and maqui berries go into jams and drinks.

Tortillas are baked under hot ashes, mültrün is a long wheat bread eaten with honey or jam, and muday, a lightly fermented grain drink, is part of the nguillatún ceremony. In Curarrehue, near Pucón, Ana Epulef, who learned from her mother and grandmother, has run the restaurant and school Mapu Iyagl since 2003, and in Santiago José Luis Calfucura opened a Mapuche restaurant in 2015.

text: Maya families in the Yucatán Peninsula and the highlands of Guatemala still eat from the milpa, the field where [[Maize|corn]], [[Beans|beans]] and [[Squash (plant)|squash]] grow together, along with root crops like [[Cassava]] and [[Sweet potato]] and fruit trees in the home garden. Corn is sacred in Maya tradition and shows up at almost every meal, as tortillas or as [[Tamale|tamales]] wrapped in leaves, and [[Achiote]] turns many dishes red.

In Yucatán, pib means cooking underground. During Hanal Pixán, families in towns like Kinchil fill [[Pib|pibes]] of corn dough, wrap them in banana leaves and bury them in an earth oven of fire-heated stones, and the first one out goes on the altar for relatives who have died. [[Cochinita pibil]], pork marinated in achiote and sour orange, is traditionally cooked the same way. In Alta Verapaz, Guatemala, Q'eqchi' cooks make [[Kak'ik]], a spicy red turkey soup the country named part of its heritage in 2007, and highland kitchens simmer pepián with toasted pumpkin and sesame, and green jocón.

text: Métis food grew out of the buffalo hunt and the fur trade on the Prairies. [[Bison]] was the main meat, dried into jerky or pounded and mixed with fat and berries as [[Pemmican]], the food of voyageurs and winter travelers. [[Rubaboo]] is a stew of peas or corn thickened with pemmican, and boulettes, meatballs of moose or elk, simmer in broth.

[[Bannock]], or galette, a flat bread of flour, water and fat, is baked on a griddle, on a stick or in a pan by the fire, and fried as beignes. Chokecherries, saskatoons, blueberries and cranberries are picked through summer, fish like [[Whitefish]] and goldeye are smoked, and [[Wild rice]] goes into pancakes.

text: The Mixteca has thin soil and few ingredients, so Mixtec cooks get a lot out of [[Maize|corn]], [[Beans|beans]] and [[Chili pepper|chile]]. From Huajuapan de León come chileajo, pork in chile sauce, mole de guajes, made with the pods of the guaje tree, tetelas, large corn tortillas filled with beans, and chilate, a spicy drink of toasted corn, [[Cacao|cacao]] and chile. Much of it depends on the chile costeño.

Goats came with the Spanish, and Mixtec families have raised them for centuries. Each October in the Tehuacán valley of southern Puebla, the matanza turns the year's goats into mole de caderas, a stew of the hindquarters with chile costeño, avocado leaves and guajes. Cooks like Olga Cabrera, from Huajuapan, now take Mixtec dishes to festivals as far away as New York.

Mixtec foodways.area: The Mixteca, western Oaxaca and southern Puebla, Mexico

text: Corn runs through Mvskoke cooking. [[Sofkee|Osafke]], or sofkee, is a drink made from hominy corn and lye, the lye dripped through hardwood ash, ideally from black jack or oak. Cvtvhakv are blue dumplings of corn dough colored with the ash of burned purple pea hulls, and grape dumplings use wild possum grapes picked in fall.

Indian pumpkin, a squash Mvskoke ancestors have grown for thousands of years, is fried with sugar until it caramelizes. The Mvskoke Food Sovereignty Initiative grows old osafke corn and Indian pumpkin from saved seed, and elders teach young people to make osafke.

text: Nahua communities speak Nahuatl, and many still farm the mīllah, a cornfield where much more than corn grows. In Chicontepec, in the Huasteca of Veracruz, fresh tlaxcalli, tortillas, are made at midday, and etl, [[Beans|beans]], go into refried beans, soups and bean [[Tamale|tamales]] called piquiz, nearly always with [[Chili pepper|chile]].

In the mountains of Zongolica, Veracruz, the Siwalcentli Collective of Nahua women shares their recipes: tesmole, a stew served with little balls of [[Masa|masa]], fresh corn tamales, tortillas cooked on a clay comal, wild greens like mixquilitl, and popotocas, insects eaten in soup or fried with salsa. Epazote, corn, squash and tiny citlaltomatl tomatoes all grow close to home.

text: Along the west coast of Vancouver Island, [[Salmon]] is the most important fish, smoked on sticks to keep through the year. When [[Herring]] spawn, cedar branches are sunk near the spawning grounds and the eggs that coat them are peeled off and eaten. Roe on kelp is gathered too, and whole herring are smoked with head and tail on. Hesquiaht's name comes from eating herring roe off eelgrass.

Clams, shellfish and sea mammals come from the shore, deer from inland, and berries, shoots and [[Camas]] bulbs are gathered in spring and summer. The west coast of Vancouver Island has had no commercial herring fishery since 2005; it's open only to First Nations food, social and ceremonial harvests.

text: Pueblo people in New Mexico and Arizona still grow corn, beans and squash, the [[Three Sisters]], for everyday meals and for ceremony, and corn holds a special place in spiritual life. Ears are roasted after the fall harvest, white corn is roasted and dried into chicos for stews, and dried, strung chile seasons much of the food.

Bread comes out of hornos, outdoor adobe ovens, and red chile with pork is a familiar dish. At Ohkay Owingeh, Norma and Hutch Naranjo teach these foods at The Feasting Place, and in Albuquerque the Indian Pueblo Kitchen cooks with [[Blue corn]], red and green chile and local produce. At [[Hopi foodways|Hopi]], cooks make paper-thin [[Piki]].

text: When UNESCO recognized traditional Mexican cuisine, it named Michoacán as the model: a way of eating built on [[Maize|corn]], [[Beans|beans]] and [[Chili pepper|chile]], grown in the milpa, made into dough by [[Nixtamalization]] and ground on stone, and kept alive by collectives of women cooks. Two cocineras from the region, Antonina González Leandro of Tarerio and Juanita Bravo Lázaro of Angahuan, traveled to Nairobi to receive it.

Around Lake Pátzcuaro and up on the Meseta Purépecha, cocineras tradicionales keep the dishes going. Corundas, a kind of [[Tamale|tamal]], come plain or with ash, chard or cheese; uchepos of fresh corn come with cream and salsa; churipo is served with plain corundas; atápakua is made with nopal or charales, small lake fish; and there are atoles of every kind. Each year they cook, teach and compete at the Encuentro de Cocina Tradicional, Michoacán's largest food festival.

sources.name: UNESCO, Traditional Mexican cuisine, the Michoacán paradigm (decision 5.COM 6.30)
México Desconocido, Ruta de cocineras tradicionales, de Santa Fe de la Laguna a Tarecuato

Purépecha foodways.area: Lake Pátzcuaro, the Meseta Purépecha and the Cañada de los Once Pueblos, Michoacán, Mexico

text: For Quechua farmers in the Andes, the native [[Potato|potato]] is the most basic food. In the Potato Park near Pisaq, Cusco, six Quechua communities organized as ayllus look after about 1,400 kinds of potato and other tubers, along with [[Quinoa]], kiwicha ([[Amaranth]]), tarwi, oca, olluco, corn and beans, and they raise [[Llama|llamas]], alpacas and guinea pigs. Families high up trade potatoes for quinoa and corn grown farther down.

In the coldest months, potatoes are left out to freeze at night and dry in the sun until they're black and hard. That's [[Chuño]], and it keeps for a decade or more. Moraya is freeze-dried in running water until it turns white. Fresh potatoes are boiled whole in their skins or baked in a watya, a small oven built of earth and heated with wood. At planting, [[Coca leaf|coca leaves]] and llama fat go into the first hole as an offering to Pachamama.

sources.name: Cultural Survival, Quechua guardians of the potato
Asociación ANDES, Potato Park, Pisaq

text: [[Maize|Corn]] is the most important crop for the Rarámuri of the Sierra Tarahumara, grown in family plots and milpas. Popped and ground, it becomes [[Pinole]] and esquiate. Many children now eat industrial meals at boarding schools, so the Rarámuri group NATIKA asked researchers from UNAM to film families making these foods, to help bring them back to the table.

Families live far apart in the mountains, and [[Tesgüino]], a thick corn beer the Rarámuri call sowiki, brings them together. Women sprout the corn, grind it, boil it for hours and ferment it in clay pots, and when the pots are opened it's first offered to Onorúame, the Father. It's shared at gatherings for healing, births and deaths, planting and harvest, ball races and house building, after the men have worked the host's fields together.

sources.name: Society of Ethnobiology, Documentation of traditional foods and agrobiodiversity of the Rarámuri (Linares, Bye and Mera, UNAM)

text: The people of Gambell and Savoonga, on St. Lawrence Island in the Bering Sea, share their language with Yupik communities across the strait in Chukotka. The Alaska Native Heritage Center groups them with the Iñupiaq as people of the north, and the sea feeds them: walrus, [[Whale]] and seal, with greens and berries from the island in summer.

sources.name: Alaska Native Heritage Center
University of Alaska Museum of the North, Alaska Native cultures guide

text: Spanish officials declared the Taíno extinct by the 1550s, but their culture survived, and today people in Puerto Rico, Cuba, the Dominican Republic and Jamaica who identify as Taíno say they are still here. Taíno words for foods and farming live on in Caribbean speech, and yuca, [[Cassava]], their staple, is still eaten, not least as a survival food when hurricanes hit.

[[Casabe]], a round bread of grated, dried cassava baked on a griddle, is still a daily food in much of the region, and in 2024 UNESCO recognized cassava bread from Cuba, the Dominican Republic, Haiti, Honduras and Venezuela, with its Indigenous and African roots. In Puerto Rico, Taíno tubers and [[Achiote]] season pasteles, and the conuco, a small farm plot, helped rural families feed themselves into the 1900s. Some young Puerto Rican farmers and chefs see these practices as a way back to Taíno foods.

Taíno heritage foodways.area: Puerto Rico, Cuba, the Dominican Republic and Jamaica

text: The Tlingit live along Southeast Alaska's coast and islands, where food comes from both the forest and the sea. [[Salmon]] is the center of the year, smoked and dried for winter. In spring, [[Herring]] eggs are gathered on hemlock branches or kelp, and [[Eulachon]] are rendered into a rich oil.

sources.name: Alaska Native Heritage Center
University of Alaska Museum of the North, Alaska Native cultures guide

text: The Tohono O'odham, the Desert People, live in the Sonoran Desert of southern Arizona. Their food comes from farming, gathering and hunting: [[Tepary bean|tepary beans]], squash, melons and chiles grown in fields watered by summer monsoon floods, and wild foods like cholla buds, prickly pear pads, mesquite beans and [[Acorn|acorns]].

In midsummer, before the rains, families gather [[Saguaro fruit]] with long poles made from saguaro ribs. The harvest marks the start of the O'odham new year, and the pulp becomes syrup, jam and wine. Tohono O'odham Community Action works to bring back traditional farming and foods, which are high in fiber and help keep blood sugar steady.

sources.name: Cultural Survival Quarterly, Enjoying a low-fat desert
Tucson Spotlight and O'odham Media, Saguaro fruit harvest sustains Tohono O'odham traditions

text: In Alaska, the Tsimshian live mainly in Metlakatla on Annette Island, where they moved from British Columbia in 1887. Their food comes from the sea and the forest, with [[Salmon]], halibut, shellfish, seaweed and [[Eulachon]] at its heart.

sources.name: Alaska Native Heritage Center
University of Alaska Museum of the North, Alaska Native cultures guide

text: The Unangax̂ have lived along the Aleutian chain and the Pribilof Islands for thousands of years, and their food comes from the water around them: [[Salmon]], halibut and cod, seal and sea lion, sea urchins, and plants and berries from the islands. Russian contact also left its mark, so tea and fish pies sit alongside older foods.

sources.name: Alaska Native Heritage Center
University of Alaska Museum of the North, Alaska Native cultures guide

text: Wampanoag gardens in southeastern New England grow [[Maize|corn]], beans and squash together, and the first green corn comes in midsummer. Corn is cooked into [[Nasaump]], a thick, filling dish sometimes made with nuts and berries. The shore gives [[Clam|clams]], quahogs, oysters, mussels and lobsters, rivers and the sea give herring, cod, bass and eels, and deer is hunted with every part put to use.

Giving thanks for food mattered to the Wampanoag and still does. Mashpee Wampanoag chef Sherry Pocknett, the first Indigenous woman to win a James Beard Award, cooks quahog chowder, three sisters [[Succotash]] and corn cakes with cranberries.

sources.name: Plimoth Patuxet Museums, What's for dinner

Wampanoag foodways.area: Southeastern Massachusetts, Cape Cod and the islands

text: The Wayuu, the largest Indigenous people in Colombia, cook from both the sea and the dry land of La Guajira: fish and shellfish, [[Maize|corn]], beans, squash, [[Cassava|yuca]], and [[Goat|goat]] above all. Friche, goat meat and offal cooked in its own juices and then fried in its fat, is made for special occasions and to honor guests, with grilled arepa, bollo or boiled yuca. The fogón, the kitchen fire, is meant to stay lit and is where the family gathers.

Corn drinks feed the family: ookostuushi, a corn mazamorra for children, and uujolu, a [[Chicha|chicha]] without alcohol, for hot days and for marriage proposals. In Manaure, Wayuu families grow kapeshuna, a small bean sown before the rains, and women save the seed in gourds until the next season. It goes into poy, a thick soup with yellow corn and lamb fat.

sources.name: Radio Nacional de Colombia, Gastronomía wayuu, platos típicos

Wayuu foodways.area: La Guajira Peninsula, Colombia and Venezuela

text: Yup'ik and Cup'ik people live along Alaska's southwest coast and up the Yukon and Kuskokwim rivers. Summer is fish camp, when [[Salmon]] is cut, dried and smoked to last the winter, and fall is for berries and greens from the tundra.
[[Akutaq]], from a Yup'ik word for "mixed together," is whipped fat with berries and sometimes fish. Dried fish dipped in [[Seal oil]] is a favorite at any time of year.

sources.name: Alaska Native Heritage Center
University of Alaska Museum of the North, Alaska Native cultures guide

Yup'ik cuisine.area: Yukon-Kuskokwim Delta and Bristol Bay, Alaska

text: In Oaxaca's Central Valleys, Zapotec women make and sell [[Tejate]], a cool drink of [[Nixtamalization|nixtamalized]] corn, toasted [[Cacao]], mamey seeds and rosita de cacao, a fragrant flower. Everything is ground into a dough and slowly thinned with water until pale curds float on top, and it's served in jícaras, painted gourd bowls. San Andrés Huayápam, which has grown rosita de cacao since the 1500s, holds a tejate fair with about 150 vendors.

Abigail Mendoza Ruiz, a Zapotec cook, has run her restaurant Tlamanalli since 1990. She cooks [[Mole|moles]], among them a pre-Hispanic mole with yerba santa, pipián of pumpkin seeds, and chicken broth with fresh corn and squash blossoms, and she gathered her recipes in a book called Dishdaa'w.

sources.name: Roads & Kingdoms, A hundred ladies stirring chocolate drinks
Remezcla, Abigail Mendoza Ruiz wants to take Zapotec cuisine to every corner of the world

text: Leached [[Acorn]] flour cooked with water in a watertight basket by dropping in hot stones, sometimes with bay or mint leaves. California Native people still make it, with both old methods and new tools.

sources.name: Phoebe A. Hearst Museum of Anthropology, Traditional acorn mush

text: Akutaq, a Yup'ik word for "mixed together," is fat whipped by hand until it's light and creamy, then folded with berries, and sometimes fish or meat. What goes in depends on the place and the season: [[Seal oil]] and sea mammal fat on the coast, [[Caribou]] or [[Moose]] fat inland. It's made for gatherings, potlatches and holidays.

sources.name: Alaska Native Tribal Health Consortium, Nellie's Recipes

text: A flat bread of flour, water and fat, often raised with baking powder, cooked on a griddle, on a stick over the fire, or in a pan. [[Métis foodways|Métis]] cooks call it galette, and it's served with fry bread at Anishinaabe sugarbush gatherings at Grand Portage.

text: A [[Diné foodways|Diné]] staple: boiling water poured over juniper ash, then [[Blue corn]] meal stirred in. The ash is a good source of calcium.

text: A round bread of [[Cassava]], usually bitter cassava, which helps it keep. The root is peeled, grated and dried, the flour is sifted, and it's cooked on a clay or iron griddle, often over a wood fire. It's a daily staple in much of the Caribbean and Central America, and in 2024 UNESCO recognized the cassava bread of Cuba, the Dominican Republic, Haiti, Honduras and Venezuela, with its Indigenous and African roots. [[Garifuna foodways|Garifuna]] women call it ereba and spend days making it to share.

text: A name for many fermented and fresh drinks made by Indigenous peoples across South and Central America. [[Amazonian Kichwa foodways|Kichwa]] women make it from boiled [[Cassava|yuca]], chewed so saliva starts the fermentation, and welcome guests with a bowl. [[Guna foodways|Guna]] women stir chicha of sugarcane juice, herbs and corn for festivals, and the [[Wayuu foodways|Wayuu]] make uujolu, a corn chicha without alcohol, for hot days and marriage proposals.

text: Small breads of [[Cassava|manioc]] flour with lard, eggs, milk, anise and often a hard, salty farmer's cheese, sold in Paraguay by vendors called chiperas and baked in a tatakua, a brick and mud oven with a [[Guaraní foodways|Guaraní]] name. Mbyá Guaraní women in Brazil make a chipa of corn, too.

text: Pork marinated in [[Achiote|achiote]] and sour orange, wrapped in banana leaves and slow cooked, traditionally underground in a pib. The [[Maya cuisine|Maya]] cooked birds and deer this way and took up pork soon after the Spanish brought pigs. It's served shredded with warm tortillas, pickled red onion and a little habanero.

text: A feast cooked in a pit on Chiloé Island, Chile. Red-hot stones go in first, then meats, clams and mussels, native potatoes and the potato breads milcao and chapalele, all sealed under Chilean rhubarb leaves to steam for about 90 minutes. In Yaldad, a Huilliche community cooks it with shellfish its own members gather at low tide, and a cooking pit on the island has been dated to 6,000 years ago.

sources.name: World Wildlife Fund, How bountiful seas could help an Indigenous community keep a thousand-year-old dish alive

text: Frybread comes out of hunger. When the U.S. government forced the [[Diné foodways|Diné]] on the Long Walk to land that couldn't support their crops, and pushed other nations off their homelands, it handed out rations of white flour, lard, sugar and salt. Fried dough from those rations kept families alive.

Today it's a powwow staple and the base of Indian tacos, and it holds both pride and pain: a sign of survival, and a reminder of the foods that were lost. It's also high in fat and calories. Some critics tie it to diabetes on reservations, while others say the deeper problem is access to healthy food, and many communities are bringing traditional foods back alongside it.

sources.name: Smithsonian Magazine, Frybread
Washington State Health Care Authority, Food and survival

text: Green and ripe [[Plantain (cooking)|plantains]], boiled, pounded smooth in a hana and shaped into a ball, served with fish soup in [[Coconut milk|coconut milk]]. Strictly, hudut is the plantain, and it's a dish that brings [[Garifuna foodways|Garifuna]] families together.

text: A spicy red turkey soup from the Q'eqchi' [[Maya cuisine|Maya]] of Alta Verapaz, Guatemala, made with tomatoes, chiles, cilantro and [[Achiote|achiote]]. It goes back before the Spanish conquest, it's eaten at weddings and other big days, and Guatemala declared it part of its intangible heritage in 2007.

text: A [[Cherokee foodways|Cherokee]] soup made from hickory nuts. The nuts are dried near the stove for a month or more, cracked, and pounded shell and all into soft balls that hold together with their own oil, which are kept frozen until it's time to cook.

text: Nitsidigo'i' in Diné: fresh corn ground into a rough dough, wrapped in husks and baked in a pit under the embers of a fire, sometimes overnight. The name comes from kneeling to grind the corn and tend the pit. Many cooks now use an oven.

In Oaxaca, [[Zapotec foodways|Zapotec]] cook Abigail Mendoza Ruiz serves a pre-Hispanic mole with corn, tomato and yerba santa, [[Mixtec foodways|Mixtec]] cooks make mole de guajes, and each October the goat matanza in the Tehuacán valley yields mole de caderas.

text: Muktuk is whale skin with its layer of blubber, eaten raw, frozen, or boiled, often cut into small cubes. In Iñupiaq whaling communities, a successful hunt is shared across the whole town.
A thick, filling [[Wampanoag foodways|Wampanoag]] dish of corn, sometimes with nuts and berries added.

sources.name: Plimoth Patuxet Museums, What's for dinner

text: Dried meat, usually [[Bison]], pounded fine and mixed with fat and often dried berries. It keeps for months and travels well. The [[Lakota foodways|Lakota]] make it as wasna, often with chokecherries, and it fed [[Métis foodways|Métis]] voyageurs and winter travelers.

text: A big filled corn dough dish, also called mucbipollo, wrapped in banana leaves and buried for hours in an earth oven of fire-heated stones. [[Maya cuisine|Maya]] families in Yucatán make it for Hanal Pixán, and the first pib out of the ground goes on the altar for relatives who have died.

text: Paper-thin sheets of [[Blue corn]] batter, made from cornmeal, ash and water, spread by hand on a hot, seasoned stone and rolled up. [[Hopi foodways|Hopi]] women make it for everyday meals and for weddings, namings and ceremonies.

text: Wild caribou are hunted across northern and Interior Alaska for meat and fat, which is dried, frozen, boiled, or whipped into [[Akutaq]]. Herded reindeer are the same species.

A starchy root that came out of South America. [[Taíno heritage foodways|Taíno]] descendants and [[Garifuna foodways|Garifuna]] women grate and dry it for [[Casabe]], [[Amazonian Kichwa foodways|Kichwa]] women ferment it into [[Chicha]], and the [[Guaraní foodways|Guaraní]] relied on it as much as on corn. text: [[Potato|Potatoes]] freeze-dried by the Andean winter. They're left out on frosty nights, trodden to squeeze out the water, and dried in the sun until black and hard, and then they keep for years, even decades. White versions, called tunta or moraya, are soaked in running water. [[Aymara foodways|Aymara]] and [[Quechua foodways|Quechua]] families both make it.

text: A small, oily smelt that runs up coastal rivers in spring. Tlingit, Tsimshian and other Northwest Coast peoples eat it fresh, smoked, or rendered into a prized oil.

In [[Nahua foodways|Nahuatl]], the treated corn dough is nextamalli. Farther north, the same idea gives [[Hominy]].

text: Oil rendered from seal blubber, a staple across coastal Alaska. Dried or frozen fish, meat and greens are dipped in it, and it goes into [[Akutaq]].

text: In Hawaiʻi, kalo is honored as an elder brother in [[Kānaka Maoli foodways]]. It's grown in flooded loʻi terraces and pounded into [[Poi]].

sources.name: National Museum of the American Indian, American Indian magazine, The breath of life

text: A desert bean at the center of [[Tohono O'odham foodways]], where O'odham stories call it the child of the Desert People. It's high in fiber and grown in fields watered by summer floods.

sources.name: Cultural Survival Quarterly, Enjoying a low-fat desert

text: [[Maize|Corn]], [[Bean|beans]] and [[Squash (plant)|squash]], planted together so each helps the others grow. The [[Haudenosaunee foodways|Haudenosaunee]] grow white corn this way, [[Pueblo foodways|Pueblo]] farmers grow all three for meals and ceremony, and [[Cherokee foodways|Cherokee]] cooks simmer them into Three Sisters stew.

sources.name: Ganondagan, About the White Corn Project
Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians, Three Sisters stew and chestnut bread

text: In Alaska, Iñupiaq and St. Lawrence Island Yupik communities hunt bowhead and other whales under subsistence rules, sharing the meat, blubber and skin ([[Muktuk]]) across the community.

Manoomin, the good berry in Ojibwe, is a native grass that grows in shallow lakes and slow streams around the Great Lakes. [[Anishinaabe foodways|Anishinaabe]] ricers knock the grain into small boats with cedar sticks, and it's food for body and spirit. It also turns up in [[Métis foodways|Métis]] wild rice pancakes.

sources.name: St. Croix Chippewa Indians of Wisconsin, Manoomin
Michigan Sea Grant, Manoomin (wild rice)
